title: Ancient DNA May Reveal the Surprising Roots of English and Other Germanic Languages - Nautilus
gist: Teaser on a Nature study led by University of Copenhagen geneticists. Using more than 4,500 ancient genomes, it identifies a previously unknown migration into Scandinavia about 4,000 years ago that coincides with the spread of Germanic languages and related cultural practices. Note: the subtitle says Iron Age, but the text dates the migration to about 4,000 years ago.

themes.theme: Ancient DNA and Germanic language origins

insights.claim: An international team led by University of Copenhagen geneticists analyzed more than 4,500 ancient genomes, 712 of them sequenced for the first time, to study the origins of the Germanic languages.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Large-scale ancient-genome sequencing is now reshaping debates that linguists have argued over for decades.
insights.quote: analyzed more than 4,500 ancient genomes (712 of which had never been sequenced before)

insights.claim: By matching identical segments of genetic sequences, the researchers found a previously unknown migration of a mysterious group into Scandinavia around 4,000 years ago.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Genetic methods can uncover population movements that the archaeological record missed.
insights.quote: a previously unknown migration pattern from a mysterious group into Scandinavia around 4,000 years ago

insights.claim: The timing of the migration into Scandinavia matches the spread of Germanic languages (English, German, Dutch, Nordic) and of cultural practices such as burial rites, architecture, runic carvings and pottery, which suggests that migration rather than cultural diffusion alone drove the spread.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Linking genes, language and culture strengthens migration-based models of how languages spread.

insights.claim: Geneticists are now joining a long linguistic debate over Germanic origins, a sign that the question is moving from linguistics to genomics.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Genomics keeps taking over long-running questions in the humanities.
insights.quote: Now geneticists are getting in on the action
insights.locator: The origins of the Germanic languages
